**Case Vignette: "Marcus"**

Marcus is a 49-year-old plumber, a big man with calloused hands and a quiet way of occupying space, as if he’s learned to make himself smaller than he is. He has been married to his wife, Diane, for twenty-two years. He comes to therapy at his doctor’s urging, after a panic attack during a routine physical sent his blood pressure soaring. He says he’s here for his health, not his head.

He doesn’t talk about the abuse at first. He talks about his work—how he likes the clear problems, the leaky pipes and broken water heaters that yield to a wrench and patience. He talks about his grown children, his garden. But in the third session, he stops mid-sentence, his hands gripping his knees. “It wasn’t Diane,” he says, his voice flat. “It was before her. Her name was Leah.”

The story comes out in pieces, like shards of glass he’s been carrying inside for thirty years. He was nineteen, a wiry apprentice just starting out, when he met Leah at a bar. She was older, confident, magnetic. He was lonely, away from home for the first time. The relationship moved fast. She was possessive, then paranoid, then explosive. The first time she hit him, he was too stunned to react. She apologized, cried, promised it would never happen again. He believed her.

It happened again. And again. He remembers the black eye he covered with sunglasses at a job site, the cracked rib he explained away as a fall, the time she threw a ceramic lamp that split his scalp. He never hit back. He was raised to believe men don’t hit women, and also that men don’t get hit. There was no language for what was happening to him. He stayed for two years, trapped in a cycle of shame and hope, until one night she pulled a knife. He left while she was asleep, taking nothing but his work boots.

He never told anyone. Not his parents, not his friends. He buried it.

Now, at 49, the past is no longer buried. It surfaces in ways he cannot control. He cannot sleep in a room with a closed door—he needs to see the exit. He wakes at 3:17 a.m. most nights, drenched in sweat, heart hammering, convinced he hears her voice in the dark. He has a hypervigilant scanning habit: every time he enters a room, he catalogs the exits, the heavy objects, the potential weapons. He avoids romantic conflict with Diane with an almost pathological rigidity; if she raises her voice, even in frustration about a bill, he goes silent, dissociates, and feels a cold numbness wash over him. He has stopped hugging her from behind, because the feel of her body turning suddenly in his arms triggers a flash of the old terror.

At work, he is reliable, even stoic, but his partner has noticed he flinches if someone taps him on the shoulder from behind. He has started refusing jobs in basements with only one exit. He tells himself it’s claustrophobia. He drinks three beers every night to fall asleep, then another when he wakes at 3 a.m. to quiet the racing thoughts. He feels a deep, corrosive shame—not about the abuse itself, but about having been a man who let it happen. He says, “I should have been stronger. I should have just walked out the first time.”

He scored a 72 on the PCL-5. He checks every box. He is exhausted, irritable, and haunted. He loves Diane, but he has never told her any of this. He is terrified that if she knows, she will see him the way he sees himself: weak, broken, less than a man. He is here, he says, because his doctor told him his heart can’t take the stress. But his heart has been under siege for thirty years. He just never had a name for the war.
